copy.headline: Danish inflation rises to 2.2 per cent as fuel prices climb

extended.text: Inflation in Denmark rose to 2.2 per cent in September, up 0.2 percentage points on August, according to figures published on Monday by Statistics Denmark, the national statistics agency. It is the first time in a year that inflation has been above two per cent.
Fuel prices drove the rise. Core inflation, which leaves out energy among other things, fell to 1.9 per cent, and cheaper holiday-home rentals, package holidays and food pulled the other way.

Mette Hørdum Larsen, chief economist at Lederne, an organisation for managers, writes that the near-removal of the electricity tax this year and next hides much of the rise in energy prices. She sees no sign yet that it is spreading to the rest of the economy. 'There is still a long way to the inflation crisis we experienced in 2022,' she writes.
Søren Kristensen, chief economist at AL Sydbank, agrees, but says prices have outpaced wages in recent quarters, so Danes have lost purchasing power.
Ulrik Harald Bie, in an analysis for Berlingske, finds households split: prices have fallen considerably for some and risen markedly for others.

copy.headline: Greenland opposition party wants a referendum on the US defence deal

standard.text: Greenland's parliament, Inatsisartut, held the first reading of the new security and defence agreement with the United States and Denmark on Monday and sent it to a second reading, which has no date yet. The vote comes only at the third reading. The governing coalition holds 19 of the 31 seats.

Pele Broberg, leader of Naleraq, an opposition party, wants the deal put to a referendum. He said it 'turns our country's importance into rights for the United States' without a matching economic return for Greenlanders. According to KNR, a Greenlandic news outlet, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland's head of government, replied that the US had put no 'offers of money on the table'.
The deal was signed on 22 September. It extends one from 1951 and lets the US set up two more military bases.

copy.headline: America threatens to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine if it hits Russian oil plants

standard.text: America will stop giving Ukraine intelligence on Russia if Ukraine attacks Russian oil plants, CNN reports. America's military delivered the warning to Ukraine's military high command at the weekend.
The threat follows a deal by Donald Trump to buy Russian diesel, which is under sanctions, to lower fuel prices in America. Strikes on Russian refineries would leave Russia with no diesel to sell.

The intelligence shows where Russian ballistic missiles are launched from and where they are heading. Without it Ukraine's air defence goes blind and more civilians will die, the chair of the Ukrainian parliament's foreign affairs committee warns in DR.

copy.headline: Venstre's leader calls the party's executive to an extraordinary meeting

standard.text: Troels Lund Poulsen, leader of Venstre, a liberal party, has called its national executive to an extraordinary meeting in Nyborg, a town on Funen, on 25 October. The agenda has one item: the current political situation.
'After some hard weeks for Venstre it is natural to gather and discuss the way forward,' Stephanie Lose, the deputy leader, told Ritzau, a Danish news agency.
The party took 10.1 per cent at the election in March, its worst result. Voxmeter, a polling firm, put it at 5.8 per cent on 21 September and 7.4 on Monday.
Two commentators quoted by Berlingske call the meeting 'uncommonly unusual' and a sign of crisis.

short.text: Troels Lund Poulsen, leader of Venstre, a liberal party, has called its national executive to an extraordinary meeting on 25 October to discuss the current political situation. The party took 10.1 per cent at the election in March, its worst result.

copy.deck: The executive meets on 25 October, after the party's worst election result and its lowest poll in Voxmeter's history.

copy.headline: Alleged hacker says AI wrote the program that took 8.7 million Danish ID numbers

standard.text: The program that took 8,749,975 CPR numbers, Denmark's personal identification numbers, was written by artificial intelligence, the presumed hacker behind the theft told Politiken. 'Any AI model launched within the past year or so could do it,' the hacker wrote. Two experts who reviewed the code for the newspaper agree that it was made by AI.

By the hacker's account, the program reached the register through a website run by Pays, a company on Funen with two employees, using a former employee's leaked password. A bug in the code searched for people born in 1877 instead of 1977, so nobody born in 1977 is in the material the hacker shared.

short.text: The program that took 8,749,975 CPR numbers, Denmark's personal identification numbers, was written by artificial intelligence, the presumed hacker behind the theft told Politiken. Two experts who reviewed the code for the newspaper agree.

copy.headline: Two American economists win the Nobel prize in economics

standard.text: Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University won this year's Nobel prize in economics on Monday, for what the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences called 'microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation'. The two Americans share 12 million Swedish kronor.

Their models show how fiscal and monetary policy can smooth out booms and slumps. John Hassler, who chairs the prize committee, said the winners' work had given 'a solid theoretical foundation for the models that are used today by central banks and governments around the world'.
During the financial crisis of 2008 it shaped central banks' monetary policy.

short.text: Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, both Americans, won the Nobel prize in economics on Monday for models that show how fiscal and monetary policy can smooth out booms and slumps.
Their work shaped central banks' monetary policy during the financial crisis of 2008.

copy.deck: Robert Hall and Michael Woodford are honoured for models that central banks and governments use to smooth out booms and slumps.
